p70: 70.  In the Court’s view, these findings cannot be regarded as unreasonable or as based on a distortion of the relevant facts. In this connection, it is important to note that, although the author referred to illegal activities on the part of certain members of the Roma community living in particular areas, nowhere in the book did he make negative remarks about the Roma population in general or claim that all Roma were engaged in illegal activities. Furthermore, in various parts of the book (the preface, introduction and conclusion) the author clearly explained that his intention was to shed light on the unknown world of the Roma community in Turkey, which had been ostracised and targeted by debasing remarks based mainly on prejudice (see paragraphs 10, 11 and 13 above). In the light of the foregoing, and in the absence of any evidence to show that the author’s statements were insincere, the Court considers that the domestic courts were entitled to conclude that the author had made a genuine effort and had not been motivated by racist intentions (see, mutatis mutandis, Jersild v. Denmark, 23 September 1994, § 36, Series A no. 298).
p71: 71.  Furthermore, although some of them were somewhat succinctly worded, the reasons given by the domestic courts in support of their findings are consistent with the principles embodied in the Court’s case-law. In particular, the courts attached weight to the fact that the book had been written by a university professor and was therefore to be regarded as an academic work. The Court has also emphasised the importance of such works in recent judgments (see Sorguç v. Turkey, no. 17089/03, §§ 21-35, 23 June 2009, and Sapan v. Turkey, no. 44102/04, § 34, 8 June 2010). Careful scrutiny of any restriction on the freedom of academics to carry out research and to publish their findings is therefore entirely in keeping with its case-law.
p72: 72.  It is also consistent with the Court’s traditional approach to examine the impugned passages not in isolation but in the light of the book as a whole, and to take into account the research method used by the author of the publication. In this connection, the Court observes that the author explained that he had gathered information from members of the Roma community, the local authorities and the police, and that he had lived among the Roma in order to study their way of life in accordance with the principles of scientific observation (see paragraph 11 above).
p73: 73.  Furthermore, it should be noted that an effective legal system for the protection of the rights falling within the notion of “private life” was in place and that the applicant in the present case was able to avail himself of it (see paragraph 68 above). The applicant was able to submit his complaints to the domestic courts at two successive levels of jurisdiction and obtained reasoned decisions on his claim. In addition, when he brought an action against the Ministry of Culture, the Ministry ordered, as a precautionary measure, the withdrawal of the 299 copies of the book in question that were still in circulation, and the copyright was transferred back to the author at the latter’s request (see paragraphs 15 and 17 above).
p74: 74.  In the light of the foregoing, the Court considers that, in balancing the competing fundamental rights under Articles 8 and 10 of the Convention, the Turkish courts made an assessment based on the principles resulting from the Court’s well-established case-law in this area.
p75: 75.  The Court nevertheless wishes to reiterate that the vulnerable position of Roma/Gypsies means that special consideration should be given to their needs and their different lifestyle both in the relevant regulatory framework and in reaching decisions in particular cases (see Chapman, cited above, § 96, and D.H. and Others, cited above, § 181). Like ECRI (see paragraph 38 above), it considers that the Government should pursue their efforts to combat negative stereotyping of Roma.
p76: 76.  It follows from the foregoing that, in the present case, the Turkish authorities did not overstep their margin of appreciation and did not disregard their positive obligation to secure to the applicant effective respect for his private life.
p77: 77.  There has accordingly been no violation of Article 8 of the Convention in respect of application no. 4149/04.
p78: 78.  The applicant argued that the expressions contained in the two impugned dictionaries published by the Turkish Language Association were insulting to the Roma/Gypsy community. He referred in particular to the expression “to act like a Gypsy”, which was defined in the dictionaries in question as “to be stingy”. He considered that such definitions, which he regarded as insulting, should be removed from the dictionaries.
